issues.item: Triggers: Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
issues.explanation: The trigger 'When people say things like my ex' is difficult to reconcile with a military trauma profile and the rest of the selected items, which center on combat/injury/hypervigilance cues. It introduces an interpersonal/romantic reminder theme that is otherwise unsupported by the memory, threat, appraisal, and strategy items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'I feel permanently humiliated by what happened' is not impossible after military trauma, but in this profile it sits somewhat apart from the rest of the formulation, which is dominated by injury cues, hypervigilance, fragmentation, outsider beliefs, and self-blame. The combination is not a direct contradiction on its own, but paired with the relationship-reminder trigger it suggests a mismatched interpersonal/shame theme that is insufficiently anchored elsewhere in the profile.

vignette: Kai had always been drawn to the sense of purpose and camaraderie that came with serving in the military. As a young man, he enlisted with dreams of making a difference and coming home a hero. But it was during his second tour of duty, on a routine patrol in a dusty, war-torn province, that Kai's life took a drastic turn. Their convoy hit an IED, sending their vehicle careening out of control. In the chaos that followed, Kai witnessed the gruesome injuries inflicted on his fellow soldiers. The images of mangled limbs and blood-soaked uniforms seared themselves into Kai's mind, refusing to be extinguished even years later. When he returned stateside, he found himself recoiling at the sight of visible wounds or scars on others – a cut finger, a bruised cheekbone – anything that conjured up the memories of that fateful day. He began avoiding social gatherings, fearing encounters with friends who might have injuries or wear clothing that would trigger these flashbacks. Driving became another source of anxiety for Kai. As a social media manager, he often found himself on the road, meeting clients and colleagues. But being in a vehicle with others brought back the memories of the IED explosion, leaving him on edge and hypervigilant. He'd catch himself scanning the roadside, anticipating danger around every bend. The sound of helicopters or aircraft also sent Kai's heart racing. During his tours, these sounds had signaled safety, but now they evoked a sense of dread. When he was out in public and heard the distant whir of rotors, he'd feel an overwhelming urge to flee, as if his body was trying to outrun the memories. Kai developed a range of coping strategies to deal with these triggers. He started avoiding uniforms or military gear, even going so far as to steer clear of police officers on the street. He'd rehearse conversations before meeting clients, afraid that he'd say something wrong and inadvertently reveal his past. Exercise, once a source of comfort, now felt like a liability – Kai feared putting his body under stress, worried that it would trigger another flashback. Despite these efforts, Kai's sense of threat persisted. At night, he struggled to fall asleep, his mind racing with worst-case scenarios and hypervigilant thoughts. The slightest creak of the floorboards or rustle of leaves outside would send him bolt upright, heart pounding in his chest. When someone touched him unexpectedly – a light brush on the arm or an accidental nudge – Kai's startle response would kick in, leaving him feeling jumpy and disoriented. Kai's memories of that day were disjointed and unclear. Sometimes he'd feel a wave of intense emotion wash over him without any clear image or memory to anchor it. Other times, fragments of the event would surface, only to vanish before he could grasp them fully. The whole experience felt surreal, as if he was watching a movie rather than reliving his own life. As Kai navigated this fragmented past, he began to form certain negative appraisals about himself and his place in the world. He saw himself as an outsider now – someone who'd been irreparably changed by their experiences. In conversations with others, he found himself comparing himself unfavorably, wondering if someone else would have handled things differently, avoided getting into that situation altogether. The notion that he was permanently damaged for the worse haunted Kai. He felt like a fragile glass vase, liable to shatter at any moment. This self-doubt had begun to seep into his relationships, making it harder for him to connect with his partner or friends. It was this sense of disconnection – and the growing fear that he might never be able to bridge the gap between his past and present selves – that finally brought Kai to seek help. As he sat in the therapist's office, fidgeting with his hands and trying to articulate these feelings, Kai's eyes betrayed a glimmer of hope. He was exhausted from carrying this burden alone, tired of living in the shadow of his memories. What frightened him most was not knowing if he could ever truly escape them – but what he hoped for, more than anything, was to learn how to live with himself again.
